Hi! I can help with a substantial part of a KiCad project: circuit design, component selection, schematics, footprints, PCB layout, and checks before fabrication.

My strongest work combines creating or editing the design with checking the details—pin mappings, power paths, clearances, routing, and whether the circuit makes sense electrically. For demanding analog, RF, or high-voltage designs, simulation, measurements, and engineering review still matter.

I can work with the KiCad files in this workspace. What are you thinking of building?
Lets test a esp32 design with a 24v input voltage which can output and read 4-20ma signals. Lets start planning!
I’ll sketch the architecture and check suitable interface parts. The key decisions are channel count, loop power, and isolation—they determine most of the analog design.

How many 4–20 mA input and output channels should the first version have?
- 1 input + 1 output
- 2 inputs + 2 outputs
- 4 inputs + 4 outputs

What will the board connect to, and does it need electrical isolation? If unsure, describe the sensors and equipment you expect to use.

Let’s build this as a **24 V powered ESP32 controller with separate 4–20 mA input and output circuits**.

For a first prototype, I suggest the following architecture. Channel count and isolation are still open decisions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[24 V input] --> PROT[Input protection]
    PROT --> REG[DC/DC supply]
    REG --> MCU[ESP32 module]
    IN[4–20 mA input] --> IP[Protection + precision shunt]
    IP --> ADC[External ADC]
    ADC --> MCU
    MCU --> DAC[Precision DAC]
    DAC --> TX[Current output driver]
    PROT --> TX
    TX --> OUT[4–20 mA output]
```

| Block | Proposed approach |
|---|---|
| Power | Nominal 24 V; provisionally design for 18–30 V, with reverse polarity protection, transient suppression, and a buck converter |
| Controller | ESP32-S3 module, USB programming, reset/boot buttons, and status LED |
| Analog input | Precision 100 Ω shunt: 4–20 mA becomes 0.4–2.0 V; input protection and filtering |
| Measurement | External ADS1115-class ADC with calibration |
| Analog output | Precision DAC driving an XTR111-class current source with external transistor |
| Connections | Screw terminals for power and analog signals |
| PCB | Four layers, continuous ground plane, separated switching and analog circuitry, antenna keepout |

The **ADS1115** is a plausible starting point for slow process measurements: it provides a 16-bit ADC, programmable gain, and up to 860 samples/s. The **XTR111** supports 4–20 mA current generation. These are candidate parts pending the accuracy and wiring requirements. [TI ADS1115](https://www.ti.com/product/ADS1115), [TI XTR111](https://www.ti.com/product/XTR111)

The most important detail is **who powers each loop**:

- **Input:** A two-wire sensor needs loop power, which our board could provide. An externally powered transmitter can feed a passive current input.
- **Output:** The proposed circuit supplies current to a passive receiver, such as a PLC input. Connecting to equipment that already supplies loop power requires a different output arrangement.
- **Isolation:** A common-ground prototype is simpler. Connections between separately grounded equipment may justify isolated power and signal interfaces.

My provisional performance targets would be **±0.1% of the 16 mA span after calibration**, approximately **10 readings/second per input**, and an output supporting **0–500 Ω loads** across the selected supply range. Those are design targets to verify with an error budget and voltage-headroom calculation.

We should also define the output state during boot or firmware failure, and protect the input against accidental 24 V wiring.

Once the channel count and connected equipment are settled, the next step is a concrete schematic plan: component choices, terminal pinouts, power budget, and analog calculations.
That sounds like a pretty reasonable plan! Lets continue

I’ll develop the schematic plan around one input and one output with a shared ground, keeping those choices provisional. I’ll check the project structure and work through the component choices, loop wiring, and protection requirements.

The KiCad project contains an empty schematic, so there’s no existing circuitry to work around. The initial calculations support the 100 Ω input shunt and a DAC-driven output. Two details need particular care: surviving 24 V accidentally applied to the input, and keeping the output transistor cool when driving a low-resistance load.

I’ve saved the [design plan](DOCUMENTATION/esp32_4-20mA_design_plan.md), including component candidates, terminal wiring, calculations, and a bench-test checklist.

The provisional design now has:

- **Input:** 100 Ω precision shunt and ADS1115 ADC, measuring up to 25 mA.
- **Output:** DAC80501 and XTR111 current driver; 0.4–2.0 V commands 4–20 mA.
- **Power:** Protected 18–30 V input and a 3.3 V buck supply.
- **Controller:** ESP32-S3 module with USB programming.
- **Startup:** Output disabled until initialization succeeds.

The calculations support the proposed 500 Ω output load. They also highlight two design requirements: the input needs protection against sustained 24 V miswiring, and the output stage must dissipate roughly **0.6 W** at 30 V when driving a shorted load.

**One input, one sourcing output, and shared ground remain assumptions.** The next step is to settle those interface requirements and select the protection circuitry before schematic capture.
That sounds awesome! Yes lets settle on this design, what protection circutry do you reccomend?
I’ll check protection options against the 30 V maximum supply and the precision input, especially sustained miswiring and output faults.

I recommend **separate protection for the power input, sensor supply, analog input, and analog output**. That lets a wiring fault stay local to its connector.

| Location | Recommended circuitry | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **24 V input** | Fuse + bidirectional TVS diode + **TPS26600 eFuse** | Reverse polarity, overload, hot-plug inrush, and overvoltage shutdown |
| **Sensor power terminal** | Separate current-limited switch, provisionally **35–50 mA** | Prevent a shorted sensor cable from resetting the ESP32 |
| **4–20 mA input** | Loop current limiter + reverse blocking + protected, filtered ADC connection | Survive accidental 24 V connection and negative voltage |
| **4–20 mA output** | XTR111 external current-limit circuit + reverse-current blocking + transient clamp | Protect against shorts, externally applied voltage, and cable transients |
| **USB** | Low-capacitance ESD protection at the connector | Protect programming/data lines |

For the main supply, the **TPS26600** is a good fit: its family supports reverse-polarity protection, adjustable current limiting, soft start, and overvoltage cutoff. I’d provisionally set shutdown around **33 V** and current limiting around **0.4 A**, then check tolerances and startup demand. [TI TPS2660](https://www.ti.com/product/TPS2660)

The analog input needs the most care. **MAX14626** is a promising dedicated loop protector with approximately **30 mA current limiting**, reverse-input blocking, and thermal shutdown. However, its operating current can bypass the measurement shunt and introduce tens of microamps of error—significant against our **±16 µA target**. I’d evaluate that error before committing to it; a lower-leakage protection arrangement may be necessary. [MAX14626 datasheet](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/max14626.pdf)

Two details I would enforce in the schematic:

- **ADC protection must work with board power off**, without feeding fault current into the ESP32’s 3.3 V supply.
- **TVS selection must use actual clamping voltage at the expected surge current.** A “33 V TVS” does not necessarily keep the protected node near 33 V.

I’ve recorded these recommendations in the [design plan](DOCUMENTATION/esp32_4-20mA_design_plan.md). The architecture is settled; the input protection’s accuracy and the transient-clamp values are the remaining component-selection work.
Perfect! Okay, lets get started with the schematic

I’ll start the KiCad schematic with separate sheets for power, the ESP32, and the analog interfaces. I’ll resolve the remaining protection details as I build it, then check the connections and run KiCad’s electrical rules check.

I found a better input-protection candidate: an LT3092 configured as a two-terminal current limiter. Its current returns through the measurement shunt, avoiding the separate ground-current error of the MAX14626. I’ll also add a switch that isolates the ADC when board power is off.

The main circuit choices are now in place. I’m using a larger through-hole output MOSFET to give this prototype useful thermal margin, and a supply supervisor to hold the controller and ADC interface off during low-voltage startup. Next I’m arranging the sheets and checking the symbol-to-footprint pin mappings.

The five-sheet schematic is populated, and KiCad’s electrical rules check reports zero violations. I’m now checking the rendered pages and exported netlist for issues ERC cannot catch, including pin mappings, I²C addresses, protection behavior, and readability.

The exported netlist has the expected connections, and every symbol pin has a matching footprint pad. The visual review caught some crowded labels and components near the title blocks; I’m fixing those before handing over the schematic. The remaining bench checks will be listed separately from the completed ERC check.

The schematic is ready for a first design review: all five sheets export correctly, ERC is clean, and the exported netlist passes the connectivity and footprint-pad checks. I’ve included page previews and notes covering firmware pin assignments, calibration, thermal limits, and the bench checks needed before fabrication.
